en: A worksheet can use three steps: locate O, read group 16, report six valence electrons, which is exactly the skill this competency names.
A rhyme can help, but the reliable method is the table position: oxygen's group is the reason the valence number is six.
Many colored tables mark oxygen as a gas on the right; that color codes physical state, while the group still codes six valence electrons.
If you draw two rings around an oxygen nucleus, put two electrons on the inner ring and six on the outer ring to match group 16.
On a shell drawing the outer ring is the valence shell; for oxygen that outer ring should show six electrons, not eight.
The competency says 'based on its position' because the periodic table is the tool: you read six from oxygen's group, not from a random memory.
Classroom wall charts often print 16 above oxygen's column; that printed 16 is your cue to write six valence electrons for oxygen.
Students sometimes copy carbon's four valence electrons onto every period-2 element; oxygen is not carbon, and its group gives six.
Another common error is giving every right-side element eight electrons; neon has eight, oxygen two boxes left has six.
Phosphorus in group 15 has five valence electrons; it is next to sulfur, not a model for oxygen, which sits above sulfur with six.
Chlorine in group 17 has seven valence electrons; oxygen is not a halogen, so do not give it seven, give it six.
Later bonding lessons use this number: six valence electrons is why oxygen so often makes two bonds or becomes a two-minus ion.
To predict the archipelago in 50 million years, first measure today's plate velocity from GNSS, then assume it stays roughly similar unless models say otherwise.
A first sketch multiplies current speed by 50 million years, converting centimeters per year into kilometers of future displacement.
The archipelago's future shape depends on more than one plate, so the method is to apply each nearby plate's velocity, not only one number.
Where crust dives into a trench it can be removed, so a fair prediction notes that some seafloor may disappear instead of simply sliding sideways.
State the uncertainty: plate speed and direction can change over millions of years, so the 50-million-year sketch is a model, not a promise.
Some methods step the map forward in smaller intervals, redrawing trenches as they move, instead of one giant jump of 50 million years.
Classroom methods can use a plate-velocity calculator: enter today's vector, choose 50 million years, and plot the predicted point.
Predict both position and shape: blocks may spread or squeeze, so the outline of the archipelago can change even if the center only translates.
Include the Philippine Trench as a boundary that can consume seafloor, a method step so the future map is not just the islands sliding as a rigid sticker.
Convert units carefully: about two centimeters per year times 50 million years is about 1,000 kilometers if that rate truly stayed constant.
Coastlines will erode and grow, so the method predicts tectonic position of crustal blocks, not the exact beach outline of today's map.
Advanced methods rotate a plate about an Euler pole instead of sliding it in a straight line, a better geometric prediction for 50 million years.
If a nearby ridge makes new seafloor, the method should add area on that side rather than only moving today's pieces like furniture.
If blocks collide, the prediction of shape should allow shortening and mountains, not just a translated copy of today's archipelago.
A method demo uses foam blocks on paper arrows: move each block 50 scaled steps and photograph the new arrangement as the predicted map.
Always write 'in 50 million years' on the sketch so no one reads it as next century; the method is geologic, not a weather forecast.
The 'current velocity' in the competency is the GNSS-measured rate, so the method starts with those published millimeters-to-centimeters per year.
The fingernail-speed metaphor is not a prediction method; replace it with a measured rate, a time span, and a drawn displacement.
